newsitem.title: FRANCE: Greek minister offers support to Albania gvt - paper.
newsitem.headline: Greek minister offers support to Albania gvt - paper.

text.p: Greek Defence Minister Akis Tsohatzopoulos pledged support on Saturday for Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino and suggested a security force set to deploy in the lawless nation might pay rebel groups for their weapons.

In an interview published on Saturday in the French daily newspaper Le Monde, Tsohatzopoulos said Greece's concern about the crisis, which he blamed principally on Albanian President Sali Berisha, went beyond worry about the Greek minority in Albania.

"Greece immediately pledged its solidarity, not only because we are neighbours or because a Greek minority lives in Albania, but because what happens there will necessarily have consequences all across the Balkans," he told Le Monde.

A revolt prompted by the collapse of popular pyramid savings schemes that left thousands destitute has left southern Albania lawless for weeks, with groups armed with weapons looted from army depots roaming the area.

Tsohatzopoulos said Athens' support was political, expressed as solidarity with the Fino government which he called the "common denominator" for Albania's political scene, as well as economic and military.
Athens has already pledged support for Fino, including the offer of a loan to the Albanian central bank for reconstruction.
Greece is deeply concerned about the crisis at its northern border, both for its effect on the Greek minority in the south and for a new wave of illegal Albanian immigrants.

Tsohatzopoulos said Greece would send "about 600" troops with the Italian-led security force, which he said should have a dual mission to disarm rebel groups as well as protecting the delivery of humanitarian aid.
The multinational force of up to 6,000 troops will try to secure the ports of Durres and Vlore and Tirana airport. It should begin to arrive in Albania from April 14.
Tsohatzopoulos said final decisions about where Greek troops would deploy were not taken but that they would not go to the south, where most of the Greek minority live.

"There are two urgent needs: one, to recuperate weapons and in my view we will not be able to avoid paying for them -- in a sense 'buy' them -- and second, to oversee the distribution of humanitarian aid."
Tsohatzopoulos said in the interview that Greece welcomed Turkish participation in the security force, but warned Turkey not to use the Albanian crisis to interfere in the Balkans.
"We do not consider that Turkey is directly concerned. Turkey is outside the Balkans," Le Monde quoted him as saying.
"What must be clear is that the situation in Albania must not be used as an excuse for hegemonic interference," he said.
Turkey has pledged about 500 troops for the force.
